title: The complete history of the Cannondale CAAD
content:
Cyclist
The complete history of the Cannondale CAAD

There aren’t many bikes that can lay equal claim to the titles ‘race bike’, ‘dream bike’ and ‘first bike’, but Cannondale’s CAAD is one. Perhaps not all of those titles all of the time, but when you can trace a design’s roots back over 40 years, it’s unsurprising that the model has gone on quite a journey.

The innovation started even before CAAD was CAAD. Back in 1983 Cannondale’s head of R&D asked his team how they could make bike frames faster.

‘Traditional frame manufacturing techniques required a lot of fixturing and tooling,’ says Chris Dodman, Cannondale’s advanced projects engineer. ‘So the guys figured that if they could get rid of the need for custom tooling, we could develop and iterate much faster.’

Todd Patterson, one of Cannondale’s first and most influential employees, was tasked with providing a solution.

‘Todd is incredible, a true polymath,’ says Dodman. ‘He came back with a method involving lasers and computer software, which was pretty wild back then. Computer aided design, or CAD, created trajectories for lasers to cut the tubes. This meant that all it took to swap between geometries was a change in programming. We could produce the tubeset for an XS mountain bike and then a 66cm custom geometry road frame one after the other on the same workstation, with maybe about a two-minute changeover. We called it tab and slot manufacturing. It was a huge investment but so revolutionary that we patented Todd’s invention and it drove our aluminium bike production all the way up to CAAD 9 in 2007.’

But we’re getting ahead of ourselves.

Back to the beginning

The first aluminium frame that the manufacturer made using the CAAD blueprint was the ST500 in 1983.

‘Compared to steel bikes at the time, the ST500’s tubes were comically oversized,’ says Dodman of a bike that was designed for road touring rather than racing. ‘But we knew oversized aluminium was stiffer and lighter than steel and titanium at the time.’

The formula proved a successful one and the diversification began. The road performance category really kicked off in 1986 when Cannondale produced the 3.0 Series, so named because the frames weighed 3lb (about 1,300g), which was uniquely light at the time.

‘In 1991 we introduced the 2.8 Series [1,270g for the frame] and the manufacturing started to get really refined,’ says Dodman. ‘Those frames had the first power pyramid, conical taper-butted down tube, meaning it had a bottom bracket diameter of about 50mm at 1mm wall thickness, and a 35mm diameter at 3mm wall thickness at the head tube. After realising how advanced our control of aluminium was becoming, some bright spark – probably Todd again – created an acronym tying the company and its material together: Cannondale Advanced Aluminium Design, or CAAD.’

Despite the ever-improving technology, convincing a traditional road bike market of CAAD’s qualities proved a difficult task.

‘Steve Berti, a colleague who has driven sales in Europe for us for over 32 years, tells it best,’ says Dodman.

‘I started visiting dealers in 1994 with our 2.8 frames,’ says Berti. ‘Most of them said thanks but no thanks. I was even shown the door by one guy who told me he sold professional racing machines, not rain gutters. In the autumn of 1996, at the World Championships Road Race in Lugano, we “unofficially” started telling dealers we would be sponsor of the Saeco-Estro team in 1997. They didn’t believe it.

‘It was a hard start to our sponsorship, but the Giro d’Italia that year changed everything – six stage wins [for Saeco], as well as Ivan Gotti taking the GC. We were called the “Dream Team” by the end of that race, and at the Milan trade show later in 1997 we had lines of dealers outside our booth just waiting to get in.’

A stellar 1998 and 1999 proved the CAAD bikes weren’t a flash in the pan, with more Grand Tour stage success for Mario Cipollini.

‘It was his four straight stage wins at the 1999 Tour de France – along with him going up to a TV camera and saying, “Cannondale makes the best bikes,” – that helped popularise CAAD bikes on the global stage,’ says Berti.

Onwards and upwards

By this point CAAD was up to version 4.

‘CAAD 4 introduced “S-bend” seatstays to encourage vertical compliance and lessen its reputation as a harsh ride,’ says Dodman. ‘The bottom bracket shell also had material removed between the threads, the dropouts had windows and the chainstays were butted, all to save weight.’

Cannondale’s production method allowed for rapid developments, so it could produce a new CAAD every year from 1996 to 2003, when CAAD 8 came out.

‘CAAD 5 was a big step, not just for us but for bringing road bikes to where they are today,’ says Dodman. ‘I think we might have been the first to switch to 11/8in steerers with integrated headsets on road. It paved the way to drop the quill stem and bring in carbon fork steerers, and most bikes still use that dimension on their steerers today.

‘CAAD 6 added an oversize bottom bracket shell, introducing the BB30 standard so we could fit our new HollowGram Si cranks – the first to use a 30mm aluminium spindle. They were 100g lighter than Dura-Ace at the time and 4% stiffer. We put Saeco through 20,000km of ride testing to validate the cranks. We later added an SRM power meter, making CAAD the first production bike with an SRM.’

Having apparently perfected the recipe, Cannondale then changed the ingredients for 2002’s CAAD 7.

‘We used a new alloy we call Optimo. It was 15% stronger than before, meaning we could make the CAAD 7 very light, but it ended up noticeably less stiff than CAAD 6,’ says Dodman.

CAAD 8 switched in a new seat tube to reintroduce some of that lost stiffness, but by the early 2000s carbon composite was showing its potential as the de facto race bike material. Metal bikes were dropping like flies in the pro peloton, but CAAD clung on longer than most, becoming the last metal bike to win the Giro d’Italia under Damiano Cunego in 2004. Cunego reportedly liked the CAAD 8 so much that the next year, when Saeco switched to Cannondale’s new carbon and aluminium Six13 frames, Cannondale just repainted his old CAAD 8 and let him carry on.

Staying power

In time, the Six13, along with the original SystemSix, did steal the spotlight from CAAD on the world stage, but Cannondale continued to invest in the platform. CAAD 9 added a bigger down tube and tapered top tube to underline its performance credentials. Despite maintaining its race bike label, CAAD recaptured its ‘first bike’ roots as cash-savvy racers began building up framesets in custom specs to suit needs and budgets. The ‘dream bike’ label came in 2009 when Dura-Ace builds were released.

‘To most other brands, dressing up an aluminium bike like that was silly, but we understood the desire for it. Besides, our aluminium could outshine early budget carbon frames significantly,’ says Dodman.

CAAD achieved a reputation as a high-performance, low-cost racer that few aluminium bikes could match in the past, and which remains today with the current CAAD 14, though the journey from 9 to 14 wasn’t exactly smooth.

‘Cannondale was bought by Dorel in 2009,’ says Dodman. ‘Frame production in Bedford [Pennsylvania] closed in September 2010. It had been running for 15 years non-stop but production was now moved overseas. We enlisted the help of outside consultants who had experience making high-end bikes in Asia and they developed CAAD 10 based on their manufacturing knowledge to our requirements. It was a complete departure from the US CAAD series that had each built on the prior model and evolved over 15 years.’

It goes to 12

To reinvigorate the platform in 2015 and emphasise a departure from CAAD 10, Cannondale skipped 11 and went straight to 12.

‘We went back to in-house design for 12 but changed the way we created the frame in the software,’ says Dodman. ‘It was the most digitally analysed frame we had ever done, with over 200 different simulations run. The top tube was tapered, not round or oval, and the seat tube was flared and very asymmetric. Every tube was pushed to the limits, helping to make it 200g lighter than CAAD 10, 10% stiffer and 50% more compliant.’

Perhaps uniquely, CAAD bikes could still compete with carbon, but that success might have been the reason 13 fell flat. Cannondale’s carbon race bike, the SuperSix Evo, had an aero makeover in 2019 and the CAAD 13, released a couple of months later, attempted to recreate the design. But carbon and aluminium have distinct material properties, and trying to copy composite in metal meant some of CAAD’s core features – smooth welds, stiffness-to-weight – were lost.

‘So CAAD 14 filtered out the too radical elements – 25.4mm seat tube, asymmetric BB30 shell, rim brake variant – and added modern features such as UDH, thru-axles and bigger tyre clearance,’ says Will Gleason, Cannondale’s road product manager and lead on the CAAD 14 project. ‘Crucially, by going back to oversized round tubes, clean welds and a double diamond frame shape, we refocused the 14 on the ride feel that has always made CAAD stand out – that balance of stiffness, comfort and razor-sharp handling.’

‘CAAD’s journey has been perfectly imperfect,’ says Dodman. ‘Without the highs and lows we might not be where we are today. Where CAAD goes in future we’re still working on, but one thing’s for sure: it will not be going away.’

Masters of metal

A brief history of the Cannondale CAAD

1983: The ST500 is Cannondale’s first bicycle, using oversized thin wall aluminum tubing fabricated with CAD software and lasers.

1997: CAAD 2 is the first road frame to use the moniker. It features weight-optimised tubing and racing geometry.

1998: CAAD 3 offers better stiffness-to-weight thanks to more aggressive machining and shaped tubing.

1999: CAAD 4 introduces ‘S-bend’ seatstays to promote compliance.

2000: CAAD 5 is the first frame to use integrated headset bearings and a 11/8in steerer tube.

2001: CAAD 6 introduces BB30 bottom bracket to incorporate Cannondale’s HollowGram Si chainset, refined with input from the Saeco pro team.

2002: A newer, stronger aluminium is used in CAAD 7. The frame gets lighter but isn’t as stiff.

2003: A revised, tapered seat tube reintroduces stiffness with CAAD 8. It becomes the last metal bike to win the Giro d’Italia under Damiano Cunego in.

2007: Cannondale continues developing CAAD while other brands drop aluminium in favour of carbon. CAAD 9 uses a bigger down tube to reaffirm its racing status.

2010: First non-US-made CAAD is introduced. CAAD 10 refines 9 and is well received, but Cannondale wants to recapture more control of the platform.

2015: CAAD skips 11 and jumps to 12, returning to US-designed blueprint. Asymmetrical tube shaping and a thin seatpost make it 200g lighter than CAAD 10, 10% stiffer and 50% more compliant.

2019: CAAD 13 attempts to copy aero makeover of the SuperSix race bike, but loses the essence of the CAAD platform and receives a lukewarm reception.

2026: CAAD 14 goes back to the design’s roots of oversize round tubes, clean welds and a classic frame shape to recapture the platform’s USP.
